A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DILLO research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendix F.

before.justification: V1 reports original MetaWorld and LIBERO experiments, including fidelity, steering success, verdict accuracy, latency, AI-judge preferences, and a human validation study.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds rejection-threshold analysis, cross-suite transfer evaluation, and steering ablations in Appendix F.

M1.justification: The proposed architecture, latent/action inputs, three-stage training objectives, and rejection-sampling procedure remain unchanged in Section 3. The new reduced-training variants and MLP critic are experimental alternatives, not changes to the proposed DILLO method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three MetaWorld tasks and five LIBERO suites. The new LIBERO-90-to-LIBERO-10 transfer experiment changes which trained explainer evaluates existing tasks, without adding datasets, task requirements, or environments.

E2.justification: V1's steering comparison uses the base policy and full DILLO models. Appendix F/Table 5 adds Stage-3-only and verdict-only variants at both model sizes, plus a latent/action MLP critic across five LIBERO suites. This substantially expands direct steering comparisons; the existing FS, ZS, and CAP comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 adds a 900-episode LIBERO-90 threshold experiment and evaluation of a LIBERO-90-trained explainer on a LIBERO-10 ACT policy. Appendix F adds training and classifier controls under a shared N=5 rejection-sampling protocol. These expand the evaluation design; the original metrics and 20-episodes-per-task steering protocol are retained. Exact threshold values are unspecified.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial component and generalization analyses absent from v1: removing preliminary training stages, removing description generation, replacing the language model with an MLP critic, varying rejection thresholds, and testing cross-suite transfer. These examine the sources of steering effectiveness and its failure conditions.

E5.justification: Section 4.4 removes the latency uncertainty reports of 248 ± 1.5 ms and 373 ± 1.3 ms, leaving point estimates. Appendix E retains the human-rating uncertainty of 3.62/5.0 ± 1.09. No new seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and existing figure results are unchanged. New Table 5 reports mean success of 71.6%/73.5% for Stage-3-only and 75.1%/72.2% for verdict-only variants, compared with 78.0%/78.9% for full 1B/4B DILLO; the MLP obtains 74.2%. Section 4.4 adds 69.5% cross-suite transfer success and threshold-dependent changes reported as +1.7% overall, +17.5% on weaker tasks, and -4.4% under heavier gating. These are added experimental results, not improvements to the retained benchmark scores.

T1.justification: Section 3.2, Equation 4 revises the sufficiency hypothesis from mutual information involving the latent state alone to mutual information involving the latent-action tuple. This changes the formal assumption to reflect the existing model inputs. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The introduction's first contribution changes the sufficiency claim from the policy latent alone to the latent coupled with sampled actions. This qualifies that claim and aligns it with the existing abstract. The main contributions concerning description generation, speed, and steering remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 replaces its task-diversity explanation for LIBERO-90 steering failures with an over-rejection diagnosis and a need for task-conditioned calibration, while removing the blanket preserve-or-improve assertion. Appendix F adds interpretations about progressive training and dense semantic supervision, explicitly acknowledging that its results do not establish natural-language generation as strictly necessary.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link in the abstract. Appendix F documents the omitted training stages, verdict-only supervision, MLP inputs, and common candidate budget for the new comparisons. It does not specify the MLP architecture or training hyperparameters; the existing parser and prompt documentation remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean's 'Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network' as support for the distillation formulation. Section 2's substantive positioning remains unchanged; other reference differences are numbering and formatting changes.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized revisions to the hypothesis and evaluation discussion, fixes the unresolved 'Table ??' reference, and adds Appendix F and its introductory pointer. Author-affiliation and acknowledgment text also changes. The overall section order and narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 5, combining retained base/full-model scores with new ablation columns. Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–9 retain their content and graphical design. Other differences are limited text reflow, reference styling, and appendix pagination.

improvement.justification: Appendix F supplies useful controls supporting staged training and description supervision, while Section 4.4 adds transfer evidence and a more qualified account of steering failures. The revised hypothesis and code-access pointer also improve clarity and reproducibility information. However, missing threshold and MLP training details and absent uncertainty for the new comparisons limit their evidential strength; removing latency uncertainty reduces transparency. The net improvement is positive but limited.
